display.purpose: Page titles only. One per screen.

body.purpose: Default prose and table cells. Cap AI narrative at 70-80ch.

bodySmall.purpose: Secondary prose, card descriptions, dense cells, the Copilot dock.

metric.purpose: The big number on a KPI card. Same size as Display, different role - never a page title.

label.purpose: Eyebrows, table headers, stat captions, nav group headings. The workhorse of the system.

mono.purpose: Machine-minted identifiers only: asset IDs, alert IDs, sensor tags, endpoints, hashes, action codes. Never human prose.

micro.purpose: Badge, status pill and chip text. Smallest step that carries meaning; steps up on tablet.

metricSm.purpose: The figure inside a compact facet tile where the full 28px Metric would crowd its container.

narrative.overview:
Forge AI looks like an apparatus with its casing off. Most industrial software hides its logic and hands you a verdict; this one renders the working as the material - detector scores, baseline statistics, tool calls, causal chains, confidence, the rule that fired. The visual system exists to make that evidence legible at speed, not to decorate it. Every surface is a place where the machine is either showing its state or showing its reasoning, and the design's whole job is to keep those two things distinguishable at a glance.

That produces a deliberately restrained world. The default surface is a warm off-white, near-monochrome, ruled by hairlines rather than shadows. Text carries the hierarchy through weight and size; colour carries almost nothing except meaning. Numbers are always tabular so a column of readings scans as a shape rather than as words. Density is high - this is software for people who read fifteen values before making a decision - but density is achieved by removing chrome, never by removing breathing room between groups.

Two colours are load-bearing and both are rationed. Forge Orange is the brand and the interactive accent. Reasoning Violet means one thing only: this was authored by the AI. A violet left border, a violet icon, a violet-tinted chip - each is a claim about provenance, and the moment violet becomes decorative the product's central promise stops being readable. The rest of the palette is machine state: green running, amber watch, red tripped.

The anti-reference is generated-looking software. Confirmed by the client: this must not read as "AI slop". That failure mode has specific tells - violet-to-blue gradients (especially on AI affordances), sparkle icons, everything at a 16px+ corner radius, a uniform drop shadow under every card, emoji standing in for icons, rainbow chart series whose colours mean nothing, centred gradient headlines, "Welcome back!" copy, abstract blob illustrations in empty states, and a grid of identically-sized tiles where nothing is more important than anything else. Two further rejections: the undifferentiated trading terminal (density without hierarchy) and the chat-first assistant (a text box where the data should be).

The underlying test is one question, and it is the most useful rule in this document. Point at any visual property and ask what it tells you. Colour tells you state or authorship. A stripe tells you severity. Monospace tells you a machine wrote the string. Tabular figures tell you the column is comparable. Size tells you importance. If the honest answer for some property is "nothing, it just looks nice" - that property is slop, and it comes out.
keyCharacteristics: Near-monochrome by default; saturated colour is state or authorship, never emphasis
Hairline borders and tonal layering instead of shadow stacks in the primary (light) theme
Tabular numerals on every figure, without exception
A 3px coloured left border as the primary severity and authorship device
Reasoning surfaces - traces, evidence, causal chains - are first-class UI, not disclosure panels
Redundant encoding for state: colour plus shape glyph plus text label, always

rules.name: The Violet Reservation
rules.body: Reasoning Violet marks AI authorship and nothing else. It is never an accent, never a chart series, never a brand flourish. When you want emphasis, reach for weight, size or Forge Orange.

rules.name: The Rationed Hue Rule
rules.body: On a screen at rest, saturated colour should occupy well under 10% of the pixels. If a screenshot reads as colourful, state has stopped being visible. Colour is how the machine raises its hand.

rules.name: The State-Is-Never-Only-Colour Rule
rules.body: Every severity is encoded at least twice - hue plus a shape glyph and a text label. In colour-blind mode the palette swaps to Wong (2011) safe values and the glyphs become visible. Because these are tokens, the swap propagates automatically - so never hardcode a status colour.

rules.name: The Warm Ground Rule
rules.body: The page is #FAF9F7, not #FFFFFF. Cards are white. Reversing this - white page, grey cards - inverts the depth model and every hairline stops reading.

rules.name: The Tint-Text Rule
rules.body: A semantic hue is the fill value, not automatically the text value. Set on a 14-20% tint of itself, the light hues fail contrast badly - Watch Yellow lands near 1.6:1 and Signal Green near 2.3:1. Text on a tint takes a darker step from that colour's tonal ramp (Watch Yellow -> #B58900, Signal Green -> #1E8E3E); Trip Red, Caution Amber, Forge Orange and Reasoning Violet pass at their token value. Verify 4.5:1 on every tinted badge, chip and pill.

rules.name: The Tabular Numerals Rule
rules.body: Every number the user might compare uses font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums. A column of proportional figures cannot be scanned, and this product is columns of figures. There is no exception.

rules.name: The Mono-Means-Machine Rule
rules.body: IBM Plex Mono marks strings the system minted. Human-written text is never monospace, and a machine identifier is never set in the body face - the distinction is load-bearing when an operator is dictating an ID over a radio.

rules.name: The Eyebrow Rule
rules.body: Every card and section is introduced by a 10px/700/uppercase label in Ink Muted. It is the system's connective tissue; a card without one reads as unplaced.

rules.name: The Shell-Never-Scrolls Rule
rules.body: The document never scrolls. Navigation, scope selector and the alert banner stay put; content scrolls inside its own region. An operator mid-triage must never lose the nav.

rules.name: The Ladder Rule
rules.body: Panel widths, radii and spacing come from the documented ladders. A one-off 37px is a defect, not a decision.

rules.name: The Flat-Light Rule
rules.body: Never add backdrop-filter to a light-theme surface. It was removed on purpose. If a light surface needs separation, use the tonal ladder or a hairline.

rules.name: The Leading-Edge Rule
rules.body: Severity and authorship live on a card's leading edge - 3px, in the semantic colour, authored as border-inline-start and never border-left. Reach for it before reaching for a shadow, a tint or an icon. Because the whole depth model rests on this one declaration, writing it physically is the single most expensive direction bug available in this system.

rules.name: The One Silhouette Rule
rules.body: 6px is the default corner. Deviating means the element is a genuinely different class of object (modal, pill, avatar), not that it wanted to look softer.

rules.name: The Stroke-Icon Rule
rules.body: Icons are 1.8px stroke on 24x24, round caps and joins, fill: none. Filled icons are reserved for the Forge mark and the Copilot node graph.

rules.name: The Latin-Convention Rule
rules.body: Uppercase and positive letter-spacing are Latin typographic devices, and the eyebrow style leans on both. They do not travel: uppercase is a no-op in CJK, Devanagari, Thai and Arabic, and letter-spacing actively breaks Arabic cursive joining. Author the eyebrow as a class whose text-transform and letter-spacing are disabled per script rather than baked into every call site.

rules.name: The Script-Coverage Rule
rules.body: IBM Plex ships genuine siblings for Devanagari, Arabic, Hebrew, Thai, JP, KR and SC/TC alongside Latin, Cyrillic and Greek, so a future locale is a subset request rather than a hunt for a second family with a different skeleton. The stack must still stay a stack, never a single hardcoded family, and each script sibling wants its own size-adjust and line-height because Devanagari and CJK sit differently on the baseline than Latin.

rules.name: The ASCII-Identifier Rule
rules.body: Machine identifiers stay ASCII and are never translated: BM-03, ALR-1024, WO-4418. An operator reading an asset tag over a radio in any locale reads the same characters. Never route an identifier through t().

rules.name: The No-Fixed-Text-Width Rule
rules.body: Never set a width on a container whose content is translatable copy. Pad it and let it size. A width in pixels around a string is a bet that the string never changes language, and this product already advertises five.

rules.name: The Earned-Stripe Rule
rules.body: A stripe is only ever earned. A card carrying no severity and no AI authorship has no coloured edge - it is a plain hairline card. This is what separates the device from the coloured-left-border callout cliche: if every card has a stripe the stripe means nothing, the page reads as a template, and the one card that actually matters stops being findable. On a healthy screen, almost nothing is striped.

rules.name: The Floor-Legibility Rule
rules.body: The desktop scale is tuned for a control-room monitor at desk distance and is too small for the plant floor. On operator surfaces at tablet width, nothing carrying meaning drops below 13px body / 12px secondary / 11px label, and the 10px eyebrow and nav label step up rather than shrink. The reader may be at arm's length, in gloves, under roof-light glare, wearing safety glasses. Density is a desk luxury; on the floor, legibility outranks it and the layout gives up a column instead of a point of type size.

dos: Do reserve Reasoning Violet (#BF5AF2) for AI authorship exclusively, and mark every AI surface with the violet left border, the Copilot glyph and a provenance eyebrow.
Do set every comparable number in tabular numerals, without exception.
Do use monospace for machine-minted identifiers and never for human prose.
Do encode state at least twice - hue plus glyph plus label - and read status colours from tokens so colour-blind mode propagates automatically.
Do take text-on-tint from a darker step of the colour's ramp and verify 4.5:1; a semantic hue is a fill value, not automatically a text value.
Do reach for the 3px semantic left border before a shadow, tint or icon when a card or row carries severity or authorship.
Do keep the page ground warm (#FAF9F7) and cards white; hairlines depend on that relationship.
Do open every card and section with a 10px/700/uppercase eyebrow in Ink Muted.
Do ration the primary button to roughly one per view; the default button is secondary.
Do pick panel widths, radii and spacing from the documented ladders.
Do end each table with the standard pagination footer, and make it actually paginate.

Do give every interactive element a real focus-visible ring and keyboard activation - this is a WCAG 2.2 AA target, and the prototype's near-universal <div onClick> is the specific failure being corrected.
Do honour prefers-reduced-motion for all of it - radars, pulses, carousels, the equaliser and the streaming text, not just the two sweeps the prototype covered.

Do author every box-model and border declaration logically (border-inline-start, padding-inline, text-align: start) and mirror directional glyphs off [dir="rtl"], so a second locale is an attribute rather than a stylesheet fork.
Do size text containers with padding and give flex and grid children min-width: 0, budgeting +35% for translation.
Do format every date, number, percentage and duration through Intl, and every count through ICU plural rules.
Do route all user-facing copy through the i18n layer, including aria-label, alt, placeholder, toasts, empty states and error messages.
Do treat an engineering unit as a property of the asset's site, never of the reader's locale; locale formats the numeral only.
donts: Don't add backdrop-filter to a light-theme surface. It was removed deliberately for contrast and render cost.
Don't hardcode a status hex. #FF453A written inline breaks colour-blind mode silently.
Don't use Forge Orange to mean a severity, or a severity colour to mean interaction.

Don't let the interface become a chat window with the data behind it. The assistant is docked, contextual and dismissible; it explains the data and never competes with it. Sparkle icons and gradient-on-everything are out.

Don't pursue undifferentiated density. High information volume is correct; a wall of monospace with no hierarchy, no whitespace between groups and colour used decoratively is not. Density is earned by removing chrome, not by removing structure.
Don't fill icons or drop below 1.8px stroke weight; the Forge mark and Copilot glyph are the only filled marks.
Don't invent a sixth severity tone. Map new states onto the five-step ladder, or give them their own axis and say so.
Don't present any figure as measured. Every number currently in the system is placeholder data pending the real APIs.
Don't write border-left, padding-left or margin-left. The leading edge is the system's primary depth device and physical declarations silently invert it.
Don't put a pixel width around translatable copy, or white-space: nowrap on a label that could grow.
Don't truncate a severity, status, or unit. Truncate values that are recoverable elsewhere; never the word that tells someone how bad it is.
Don't concatenate translated strings or interpolate a plural by hand; a sentence assembled from fragments cannot be translated.
Don't hardcode a single font family. The stack must remain a stack so script-matched faces can be appended.
Don't convert an engineering unit because of a locale. A threshold of 12.5 mm/s becoming 0.49 in/s without the canonical value alongside is a safety defect, not a formatting choice.
